reviews.text: I wanted this to be leaning more into being an immersive sim; that's on me. It [i]isn't[/i] an immersive sim in the slightest. This is an obscenely shallow game: it's basically just 'showdowns', which are spit-and-it'd-reach-the-other-side arenas full of hit-scan/homing shots that force you to spend most of your time trying to re-locate shouting at your monitor screen in disbelief due to all the bullet spam coming from the tiniest angles, heat-seeking the pixel you've got overhanging. ...and that's it: that's the whole game. The 'roguelike' elements amount to barely anything. You don't feel like you're in control or that you're actually 'getting somewhere'. The crew 'feud' system gets into a death spiral, and there's never enough beans. ...and [i]good Gawd Almighty[/i] it's fricken annoying being blasted by heat-seeking shots you [i]cannot[/i] avoid without having terrain in your face. ...but you can't even do that because there's a load of mechanics in play to [i]force[/i] you to move...right out of your safety spot where you're trying to hide from the deadliest goons you've ever known whilst [i]your[/i] character's shots make you second guess if the characters drunk. And no, it isn't 'too difficult for me' - the game is lacking a 'dodge' mechanic. If you couldn't dodge attacks in DOOM Eternal or Dark Souls it'd be brutal. [i]This[/i] is just bad game design. I honestly - and I hate to say this - wish I could refund this. The base idea is sound, but it's so badly executed. I guess I have to hope they, y'know, see sense and buff this up slightly?

Anyone coming into this game expecting Void Bastards in the Wild West, you're setting yourself up for disappointment. What you instead have is the perfect bite-sized game. As someone who is often jumping into and out of play sessions, I can say there is definitely an audience for this (and I'm it). Managing the overworld map is picking one point at a time, and beaming down. Once on a planet, you manage your team of Bastards a few squares at a time, trying to min/max getting as much loot as you can while picking as many fights as safely possible, with an eye on a timer that says it's time to GTFO. Firefights occur on a wide variety of biomes, with several modifiers and enemy types to keep things interesting, but the longest I have had one last would have been 5 minutes. Even gear management and relationship management for the outlaws is bite sized, with no more than 3 gear and a simple "Are they pals, meh, or nope?" that can be altered in the press of a button - provided you have the magical beans. Beans, beans, the magical fruit, the more you eat the less you feud. I'm leaving that in. Bonus points for the writing, the humour is for a specific type of person (this is where being the spiritual successor to VB comes in, imo, along with the constant sense of forward motion while being a loot goblin) but the dialogue feels very authentic - the actors definitely enjoyed themselves and it shows. All the Bastards play differently, and as you get more Aces for them you can really start to feel less like just a gun with a voice attached to it, and more like an entire unit/character that you can plan around. Seriously though, this might be the epitome of Steam Deck play - pick the game up, spend 10 minutes taking 3 turns on a planet and winning (hopefully) 3 showdowns and then you put it down, and it'll be there waiting for you to come back like a Bushwhacker behind a door. If polished jump-in, jump-out action with a side of usin' yer noggin is your thing, give this a try. You won't be disappointed.

TL;DR: While it may not be for everyone, to me this is a fantastic strategy game with engaging showdowns peppered throughout. Two things that you should be aware of before you play this game: [h2]1. This is NOT an FPS game with a Strategy System. This is a Strategy game with an FPS System[/h2] [h2]2. This is NOT Void Bastards.[/h2] To address point 1, while the screenshots and trailers seems to suggest that this is a First Person Shooter first and foremost, it is not. The real meat and potatoes of gameplay is the strategic movement across two kinds of procedurally-generated maps (planetary and interplanetary) and the management and careful application of your crewmates and resources. While the gunplay that you participate in can be fun, engaging and challenging, you're actually better off avoiding fights when you can so that you can be best prepared for the fights you can't avoid. To address point 2, no really, this is NOT Void Bastards. While it shares its DNA in terms of its writing, visuals, personality, charm and Challenge, this is a very different game when you're actually controlling the player characters. While in Void Bastards, you are crawling around in cramped, maze-like ships laying traps and sneaking past enemies in a timed scenario to find the most loot, in Wild Bastards you are often placed in wide open areas with the sole objective of finding the most survivable way of killing every enemy in the encounter, strategically locating enemies and dispatching them with the tools at the disposal of the two Bastards you chose to fight with. If you are expecting Void Bastards 2, you may want to give this one a miss.

This like the original Void Bastards was a game i had a lot of hype for and was hoping they would take the lessons learned from that game to make a better game in the similar style which looking back, Void Bastards issue was its length only because of its abrupt ending, so when i picked up this game lemme tell you i was surprised to see a completely different direction with this game. Now this is not a bad game, but between the two Void Bastards is the game i like more. Where Void Bastards thrived in having you with the bare minimum to protect yourself, and throwing you into dangerous environments to scavenge for scraps, this game gives you everything you realistically need to wipe out every encounter with ease, and because of that most of the planet maps are a bit of a breeze to go through. There were about 3 planets back to back to back where i pissed off all 3 big bad scary enemies that are designed to make you extract off the planet and i just went through with judge and killed all of them as they dropped down. Unfortunately the biggest thing contributing to me not wanting to get back into the game is the base shooter game play, If you have played Void Bastards you know its a very slow, almost tactical experience where you have to move slowly, avoid getting hit, and making your shots count, and this was enhanced with the claustrophobic maps with imposing enemies that will block you're routes you attempt to take, now imagine all that but instead of being in a tight map, you are in a big ass open arena with little bits of cover and scenery, sometimes its a canyon, maybe your on a mesa, or sometimes you're in a big ass mine. Now it does have an interesting character mechanic that allows you to use different character with different guns and abilities which is cool to swap between them, but its still doesn't help how clunky it feels as it turns into Lore Accurate Cowboy fights where you just end up sitting if cover until the enemy has to reload and then you just kill them right then and there, and repeat for maps with sometimes up to 16 enemies, not to mention most of the times the enemies just kinda teleport into the map randomly. Now double unfortunately everything else about this game is awesome, the art style has this sick Sci-fi Tron Cowboy thing going and its does really well with it through the whole game. The different characters as i said are cool to swap between through with a neat Fued mechanic where if two characters don't like each-other you can't bring them on the same planet, this ended up making me have to solo the first bit of the game as Judge as no one likes that guy even though he is literally the coolest thing ever. Now I'm not saying this game is a full dud if your at all interested in it i would totally recommend buying it but if you're like me and were hoping for what was described as "The spiritual successor to the award-winning game Void Bastards" i would look elsewhere this game took the art style and the gun-play from that game and ditched everything else that made it good.

This game does one thing and it does it very well. The gameplay is absolutely addicting. When I first booted it up, I didn't think I'd be into it as I'm not usually into arcade style First Person Shooters. Once i got into the groove of a few of the characters there was no going back. This game consistently throws new characters, enemy types, abilities and gameplay modifiers at you to keep things fresh. The story is interesting enough but pretty barebones. That said, the characters are all pretty humorous and are fun to get to know as the game goes. Now it's time to go play Void Bastards.
Highly recommend if its on sale. If its not on sale, I would not recommend though.

Oh how mighty has fallen. I've enjoyed Void Bastards - to a degree. The game has become too repetitive on in the middle-final stretch but it still felt a good mixture of action and stealth albeit a bit badly executed at times. But the art and gunplay was good so I've enjoyed it. Now comes Wild Bastards - forget what you know about Void Bastards - the characters are all set, not randomized. The 'levels' are even smaller than those in Void Bastards. And more importantly - the gameplay? Absolute dogshite. Forget hunting down components or resources while making a run for it. 90% of your time is gonna be spent planning where to move next on the map and hoping your enemy won't do something brash... and that's the problem. The systems don't work in unison. What worked relatively OKAY in Void, got replaced here by plentitude of systems that just don't work well together. This is not helped by the fact that the little combat instances are not fun. Sometimes you can spawn in and immediately get gunned down by turrets. That's it. Or ganged on by a whole team of snipers. This isn't fun, this is tedious. Normally I would say that "I didn't like it but maybe you'll like it". Here I'll say - "Avoid.":

Although there is a lot of fun to be had I can't recommend Wild Bastards due to glaring issues with the price, the story, and the gameplay. We aren't given much information from the start but suddenly after a few hours we're supposed to hate certain characters that have only been good in our eyes. The game suddenly forces Fletch on you and she comes off as an irritating marry sue who knows all and suddenly has control over the plot while being a useless piece of ♥♥♥♥ herself. The end game is just out of left field and ruins the flow of everything by forcing you to play outside of the play style you have been developing for the whole game. All the combat encounters are painfully short to the point of being 60 seconds or less in some cases which ruins the little bit of flow you manage to get going. The game never tells you that characters don't level up based on usage but based on card collecting. For most of my playthrough I skipped the cards thinking they were optional only to get them at the end and randomly get characters I hated being higher level than characters I loved since cards are character specific and generate randomly on a planet's surface. This game is also way overpriced compared to what you get. I got on sale for about 8 bucks and that was as much as I'd ever pay for it. If you see it on a steep discount then maybe give it a shot but go in with low expectations.

Void Bastards was one of my favourite games and I have bought it on multiple platforms and played through a few times. So I was keen to see what this dev would do next. But this game shows they didn't understand what made Void Bastards fun. Wild Bastards is just just boring and uninteresting and I can't recommend it to anyone.

I hate to be like "the problem is that it's bad," but that is the problem. I loved Void Bastards. A grimy, nihilistic looter that encourages you to circumvent problems when you're not crashing straight through. And I do like Wild Bastards' visual presentation---mostly. Its environments are full of little niches you have to check, and they don't look nearly interesting enough to have to scan hundreds of them to clear each map. Wild Bastards changes up its looter runner gameplay for western shootouts, but doesn't have the chops to make those shootouts fun. And it's at a pretty fundamental level where the problem is. This is supposedly a precision shooter, but your shots on most characters are either a) RNG, or b) not good and the whole character is not good as a result and this is 90% of the cast actually. So, you'll use your gunslinger with dual pistols to try and pop someone from a distance and you'll click directly on them and they'll be standing still and your shot will scatter a random amount and miss---and then they'll turn around and bullseye you instantly, because they don't have to deal with that. Also, I know how I said the core fps gameplay was fundamentally broken, but that's only when you see it, because most of this game is menus. Menu to select a planet, menu to move between nodes on a planet, menu to group up your characters on the nodes on the planet, menu to interact with each node, menu to advance the day/night cycle, multiple downtime menus when you go back to your ship to equip and feed beans to your crew---although feeding beans doesn't matter too much because it gives a sometimes buff when you take damage enough times, and this benefit goes away often and at random. There's also a LOT of story, to the point where I'd say this is not a roguelike, it's wearing one like a costume. It wants to be a narrative shooter, and it probably should have been. If it was built like a traditional fps campaign, you could have levels where you use the bad characters because the levels are built for them. For example, the snake cowboy could have a series of rooms with only one weak enemy in them that has no hit points, no attacks, and no effects. He would shine under those conditions. Well, not shine. Struggle less. He might still die. But it would be possible to play him at least. The other issue is that gameplay feels clunky and slow. I mean, the menus, sure. And the whole cast yapping 24/7, that also. But when you get into a fight, a lot of enemies have behaviors like "stay put and don't make a sound" so you have to bughunt the whole map to clear it, and sometimes you'll just get surprise killed by a shotgunner hiding in a blind corner up a ladder that you can't do anything about because climbing a ladder gives you teleport induced blindness and plays a damage sound effect so you can never tell if you've gotten got the instant you climb up one. This kind of design should make Wild Bastards feel kind of hard and random, but to offset that you simply replay any sector you fail to clear. So. Uh. Just sandbag until you level your characters fully I guess? Normally I'd give a game more of a shot, but the problem here is the basic feeling of play. That's not going to improve. If you're really curious, maybe try this on a deep sale? But I'd strongly recommend Void Bastards instead.

I see a lot of reviewers complaining that this is not Void Bastards. Well, it is definitely not. First and foremost—this is not an immersive-sim roguelite. This is an FPS roguelite (with lite RPG elements). Comparing it to Void Bastards is wrong because, despite having the same devs and similar visual style and premise, the core of the game is totally different, and the gameplay is something else completely. Is Wild Bastards a good roguelite FPS? It is interesting for sure, but sometimes I have a feeling that the game is a bit undercooked or unbalanced, and some systems don't feel well thought-out or polished: 1) Encounters with enemies feel more like a chore than exciting showdowns. A lot of enemies are hiding or even using invisibility, and sometimes you see an opponent only after getting hit. The game feels more like a stealth shooter, where giving out your position usually comes with punishment, like half of the map going into blind rage and attacking the player. With little TTK and high damage, this is not a very fun experience. 2) Shooting itself feels hollow and impactless. Everybody got used to gunplay being weak in immersive sims because those games have a good amount of other cool stuff. But Wild Bastards is FPS, and the gunplay from Void Bastards is not enough here, sorry. 3) You have 13 characters, but the game never really gives incentives for players to try everyone. I played 20 hours and beat the campaign on hard, but did it mostly with half of the roster; two characters I played only once, and one character (Rawhide) I haven't even played a single time. You can say it's the player's choice to try different things or stick to the same old, but you actually upgrade characters with mods and skills, so trying someone new without upgrades is giving yourself a disadvantage. 4) Balance. I don't expect ideal balance with 13 characters, but some of them are just OP. Smoky and Casino have ultimates that just kill enemies on the map without even needing to see them; that makes them much stronger than everyone else. Sarge spots and highlights enemies, which is crazily effective in a game where every opponent tries to hide and be sneaky. There are other issues too, but you get the idea. All complaints aside, the game is fun, and I beat it on hard in 20 hours without getting bored. Frustrated? Yeah, sometimes. Not because the game is hard (I failed sector only two times), but because Wild Bastards just shows its rough edges and lack of gameplay polish. And when I say lack of polish, I mean game design and idea implementation. Optimization is good in this game, and there are no bugs, so in the technical aspect, Wild Bastards is actually perfect. I recommend Wild Bastards; it is fun and tries something different and exciting, but some things here needed more time to cook.

I had a ton of fun playing Wild Bastards! -The character design is pretty wicked--each character has their own weapon and special ability that synergizes well against certain kinds of enemies (Except for Ros, i stg). Figuring out who beats what is one of the great joys of the game, as every character gets their chance to shine. The game is fully voice acted, and your characters will talk to each other mid-battle, so neat! -The world map part of the game is fun. There are some elements that trivialize it (Casino's money on kill, Hopalong's bonus movement speed, Energy being essentially ignorable), but it rarely feels unfair. Sometimes it puts you into tough situations, which I think is cool, but not too often (not often enough?). -The art, music and level design are amazing, nothing subtracts from the experience, eveything adds. -The story is honestly... weak. But the gameplay is solid and fun. I say add it to your wishlist and grab it when its at a good price. You wont regret it!

There is enemies that have bullets that lock on, the feuds are annoying, judge and hopalong are pityful. Game is blanketed in darkness too often and poison damage is over powered. Just unfun and the constant interruptions when the chaser shows up, who is weak as ♥♥♥♥ so not a concern.

meh. It's not void bastards. It became repetitive and boring very quickly. No loot means I can exit asap, which ironically means I can quit as soon as I want. For me that was 2 hours. I would rather play void bastards and scavenge for pens while hiding and sniping. This game seems to be for people that don't know games and this is their first game... think duck hunt.

Personally, this game feels unusual to me & I still don’t fully understand how all the colors work together. I come from playing games like Max Payne, GTA, Call of Duty, Alan Wake, RDR, where the gameplay & visuals are grounded in something close to real life. For example, when you see a tree in those games it looks natural leaves, wood, everything you expect. But here even something as simple as tree leaves can look like neon glow. That’s just one example. Despite that, I have actually come to enjoy the game. It feels like a quick jump in & fight type of experience which works well. The visuals are still strange to me but I can tell there is a very distinct creative thought process behind the art style. It’s just very different from what I m used to.

This is not an FPS game and I feel it is deceptively named and marketed. Void Bastards was a rogue like FPS with decent mechanics. This is a visual novel gluing together a board game with the cracks filled in by a bare bones hide and seek fps minigame. There is a tremendous amount of yapping and board game stuff and inventory and dialogs and interfaces, I am spam clicking 50+ times to get to gameplay. The shooting segments are not fun. They're big open randomly decorated areas with a handful of dudes hiding in them. You spend minutes looking for them, then shoot them for 1 second. Or they shoot you from behind and you die. Ladders are everywhere and implemented as instant warps which makes player and enemy movement clunky. I entered a big open arena where worms spawn at random and shoot you in the back for 50 poison damage per shot and I lost 2 guys. I entered another big open arena with dogs that instantly spawn in and shoot you from all sides with no cover at all and lost the third guy. I healed and retried, another arena with poison worms that shoot you from all sides for instant death. I'm done.

It feels like im missing something. The gameplay is boring :/, the fights are bad and unfair, the mechanics and characters feels simple, or uncomplete. I constantly felt like if you added a little more depth to some mechanics it would be such a good game, a shame. And i gotta complain specially on the way you interact with the levels, like, moving around the maps with restricted turns and moving distance is cool, plus you add the rush of the boss, but you rapidly see all of it. Then you add the fact that you do that also in the ship every planet and you are clicking so much buttons that i feel like there's friction for me to get to the fighting (fun part?).

There's so much stuff explained in the tutorial, but nowhere to go back and reference it. -UI can be confusing -Why tf do our items disappear between jumps? Makes literally no sense, especially for a roguelite type of game -Voicelines are cringey and McNeil talks too much. Every time I encounter McNeil, he has 4 or 5 lines of dialogue and all of it is pretty annoying to listen to, so I skip it. -The Laser enemies have hitscan against you. They shoot at you and hit every time. (Maybe I'm just bad at dodging it.) (Will revise as I play more) My current rating is 7/10 Still fun, just has some issues.

I had really good fun with this. It's not Void Bastards 2 and that seems to have annoyed some people, but it's still a fun game when you are actually in a battle. I had no idea what was going on with the story as characters popped in and out of my roster for some reason, but I also didn't care because the characters have quite different abilities and the actual FPS part is fun. Looks good as well and ran very well on the Steam Deck.

I liked the story, I liked the theme and I liked getting to know the characters, their mechanics and whatnot. On sale it is a good game for around 10h of non-boring gameplay. After that, after finishing the campaign, I do not feel drawn to replay the game, try the procedural campaign or the challenges... I continued playing after getting all the characters because I wanted to finish it, not because I was properly enjoying it. Combats feel like a drag after a while, and it feels like doing it just to see the next ace and the finish the next system. I enjoyed it, yes, and I recommend it if you want to have around 10h of fun. But at the full price of 35€ I can't recommend it...

I am a big fan of Void Bastards, it was a great, enjoyable experience gameplay ad design and artwork wise, Wild Bastards gives me more of what I fell in love with, but.. different? Can't say it's bad, it's a mix of new and old.. IT IS NOT VOID BASTARDS 2, get into this game with that mindset and you'll find it enjoyable I am sure.

Got it on sale so for me it was definitely worth the price. It's a fun fast, pace roguelike with interesting twists to mechanics. The art style is fun and the "Bastards" are all unique and exciting characters to play. This game rewards you the more you challenge yourself so that is always a hit of dopamine. A few small downsides. First, you don't get alot of the more fun, strong characters until the end of the main story. I understand it's for balance sake but it still sucks to get like Rawhide when you've been forced to use Rosa majority of the game. I also think the randomness of the perks or "aces" are a little unbalanced. Some perks are OP and immediately add layers of fun while others are just a simple upgrade. I've played a bunch of different roguelites and -likes so I understand that mechanic but fundamentally is always a flaw. Bottom line, I enjoyed this game and I recommend you at least to try it

I've really enjoyed the game! I was a big fan of void bastards and picked this up when I saw it on sale. It took me a bit to really get into but once I had a few characters I had a blast and it made me really want to mess around in the post game! I think all the characters have fun gameplay and you can tell they wanted even more character in this game than their last. Really looking forward to Godzone 6!

While core gameplay loop is fun the awful map layouts and random enemy spawns is what kills it for me. Too many times i was have a sniping duel with a enemy only for another enemy with a shotgun to teleport up a ladder (there's no climbing animation or climbing sound effect) and i would die in a nano second because you have to rely on the enemy yelling at you in order to keep track of them. Void Bastards is a way better game.

I think they did a great job infusing strategy and gunplay, there are times in this game where you just run through everything instantly and times where you might take 15 minutes to finish a showdown depending on your line up and the enemy line up. I enjoyed my run through on hard and will be coming back soon to try the hardest difficulty. Great voice acting too, the characters feel unique and have great interactions. One thing I do agree with, pick this up on sale, as I did. I'm not full convinced of its value at full price but I picked it up for 7 bucks on sale and found it VERY much worth that value. If you liked void bastards and wanted a bit more of a strategic approach, you will enjoy this game.

So, first off, this is not Void Bastards 2. This is a space western about a band of outlaws getting the gang back together for one last hurrah before riding off into the sunset. Wild Bastards plays more like a board game where encounters are resolved by first-person shooting. It's a weird game, it's like one third conversations between space cowboys, one third moving your piece around a map, and one third gunfights. If you're looking for a first-person shooter this might not be the game, like I think to get the most satisfaction you have to like the Bastards and have fun trying out goofy combinations of outlaws. And beans, you have to like beans.

horrible! I paid 7$ and still feel ripped off. They had such an amazing formula with Void Bastards but they took the most frustrating elements of that game and turned it into one. The rng in Void made it tense and fun. The rng in this makes it feel frustrating and broken. The world is less interesting. The maps are less interesting. Man this one hurts to write because I had such high hopes for this game. The game is a roguelike where you collect new characters and add them to your posse. Thats it, thats the entire game. Theres not really a story besides some idle chatter. Theres a pointless board game with moves that just seems to waste a bunch of time, you collect some stuff, then you spawn on a small map and just have to kill the 4-10 people that spawn there. Theres 4-5 total environments, all of which are basically empty with some buildings for cover and high ground and thats about it. You do this for like 4-5 levels then collect a person and add them to your party. Then do this for 15 hrs or so over and over and thats the game. The fun part is getting all the characters and seeing how they play, and they are very different. But even that could have been done better. All characters have 1 weapon and 1 special power, and thats it. You level them up and collect gear but its only stat bonuses, you'll play the same with every character from when you first get them until the end of the game. Upgrading characters with new weapons, alternative fire, or new powers would have kept things novel. You fight the same enemies throughout the game as well. The game adds annoying factors to prolong game length. Theres a charge meter which is a good idea because it keeps you from using certain guys too much. But then also for no reason some can get lost during landing meaning you need to go and rescue them, this being the people you have already rescued originally in the game earlier. Oh and 2/3 through the game 75% of your team gets recaptured and you have to go RESCUE THEM AGAIN......WTF?! Oh and theres this useless feud system that for no apparent reason characters suddenly can't be q'd together, which was already addressed with charge, so why add this useless constraint as well. All of these systems just seem to add more annoyance and prolong the barebones game. Then after rescuing everyone again and then rescuing more random people that aren't even characters the game just......ends. Theres no boss fight, no real anything. I kept looking up how to beat the game because the game just felt so repetitive and arbitrary that it just kept going after I rescued everyone, but thats this game in a nutshell. The look and feel of the game is decent, and impressive varied character creation that all have a unique feel. But the rest of the game is a repetitive, shallow, boring slog. 6/10.

Was a big fan of Void Bastards so was immediately interested in this wacky looking game. If you like one you'll probably like the other. The unique style and humor is all here and the dialogue is half the reason to play the game. The voice acting is top notch and looking forward to the interplay between the characters kept me playing moreso than the actual gameplay. It was a lot of fun building out the outlaws in different ways. I was surprised when you lost all your equipment between sectors initially but ended up liking the mechanic as it often challenged you to play in unorthodox ways using what could be immediately scavenged. The campaign is truly a campaign. My first successful run took probably a week to complete. If you are looking for short rouge-like runs, this isn't that kind of game. The only meta-progression really comes from unlocking different pieces of equipment by either beating the game on a particular difficulty (unlocks lower as well) or completing a challenge. The challenges are pretty weak, I'd say I only really enjoyed one of them. They seem mostly the same, it's only a single sector and you start with different outlaws, that's about all that is different between the majority of them. The overall story also kinda just faceplants at the very end with no real conclusion of any kind. You never even fight the big bad dude chasing your outlaws around. The dude maybe has 4 voice lines in the entire game. There is such an interesting world here and it is barely explored at all. There are small QoL issues as well. Certain things that can't be skipped, like when a posse lands on a planet to chase you. It can happen up to 4 times each planet, average 6 or so planets each sector, 100s of sectors. The point is, it gets old having to wait the 8 or 10 seconds every single time it happens. It's the same when you get the infamy rewards at the beginning of each sector. Have to wait for the bar to fill every time. It even slows down as it gets closer to the end so you really get to build the suspense each time. Planet variety also gets pretty stale after awhile, even though I like a lot of the arenas. I think there are 6 total? These aren't gamebreaking problems or anything. Minor inconveniences really, but it seems like they add up in this game, which is unfortunate because there is a lot to like here. I'd love to see a sequel or some DLC. I really enjoyed my time with Wild Bastards but unless more content is added, I doubt I'll ever feel the need to revisit it other than to chuckle over a remembered voice line.

Initially, I was lukewarm on Wild Bastards. The narrative felt a bit meh and the game veered on easy on Normal difficulty. These combined made the experience be a bit repetitive and cardboard-y. But the excellent audiovisual style and the colorful characters kept me going until the end. Was going to agree with another reviewer that it was not as good as Void Bastards. But then, on a whim, I decided to do the challenges. And immediately the game experience changed; Having a limited amount of Bastards (which are effectively weapons with a different HP bar attached that you can switch between) to perform the challenges made things more tactical, and the map movement more relevant. Once the difficulty was upped, and you had to [i]think[/i], the game clicked. Inspired, I did the max difficulty, perma-death-ish mode on (which was also interesting, since it's not necessarily permadeath in a traditional sense. If you go down, you lose access to the Bastard, until you get an item to revive them. You only lose when you lose everyone simultaneously), and it was tense, exciting and tactical. I had to rely on weird combos if I lost too many Bastards. If I had something to complain, the Collector achievement is annoying, since there is no way to track what you have gotten, on higher difficulties the enemy pool gets kind of samey and pushes towards specific strategies (Armor shredding is a must), and the late-game Bastards feel a bit less effective, since you have less experience with them. But the procedural campaign fixes that. So, eventually I recommend this. Click the permadeath notch on and up the difficulty a bit.

Being a fan of Void Bastards I of course had to try Wild Bastards. After finishing the campaign I can say it is not like Void Bastards, but it has it's own charms. In the beginning I always compared Wild B. to Void B. and found it lacking. The combat was tough, but I felt like I didn't make progress. Moving from Planet to Planet and unlocking a few modifications and Aces, only to lose thos modifications at the end of the Sector made me feel like I was stuck in a hamsterwheel. I stopped playing there for a while, but later came back to the game as I want to finish what I paid for. And the game did actually change. I don't know when, but I noticed over time that I was having more and more fun with the game and sometimes even more so than with Void Bastards. The reason seems to be that over time the Aces that you collect really do change how the Bastards feel to play. Instead of having just different weapons, the Bastards becomes specialists of certain kinds of combat or against certain enemies. While also becoming stronger in general. While at the start I felt like I was always at a disadvantage, later on it felt more like a shooting gallery. And that wasn't a bad thing at all! The shooting gameplay became light, fun and quick. It is an arcade shooter and not at all realistic. And as I got stronger I could actually enjoy that, instead of feeling hindered by it. I really noticed that after finishing the campaign, when I tried a challenge run. Being send back to the beginning with weak Bastards was a slap in the face. With my experience I fared a lot better, but it did feel like a grind again, not like I was playing a game for fun. And another thing is that the dialogues only get better the more Bastards you have. Probably because I liked the later Bastards more, anyway. It's unfortunate that I found Spider Rosa and Doc Casino to be some of the more unlikable characters of the crew. But soon you get Smokey and he carried the crew for a while, in my opinion. The game takes a while to get going, but once it picks up, it is a lot of fun.

I'll give Wild Bastards a soft recommendation. One of the things I loved about Void Bastards was exploring the procedurally generated ships, and taking advantage of im-sim style environmental elements on board. It wasn't perfect, but it's what kept a lot of my attention about the game. By comparison, the first-person experience in Wild Bastards feels much shallower. The arenas which generate for every fight hide enemies and combat pickups. Each fight shouldn't take more than a couple minutes. Once you're good enough at the shooting (and avoiding taking damage from enemies whose shots are often very quick & accurate), the "game" part of the game becomes much more about resource management, as you seek to stockpile long-term advantages. The deep-space cyberpunk wild-west theming is fun, and I enjoyed getting to know some of the characters. Many of them are written with endearing and unique personalities that I enjoyed. And there's a TON of characters. So those of you who played Void Bastards who wanted a more story and character-driven experience, well you'll find it here. There's also essentially no permadeath, so it's not a roguelite at all similar to Void Bastards' format. But, and not to be a broken record, the thing I really miss is any sense of immersive exploration at all. I had a good time, but I was hoping for that vibe. It's not really fair for me to hold it against the game though for expecting it to be something it never promised. Maybe with proper expectations from this review, you'll be able to look past it a little better. It's easier for me to recommend Void Bastards, but I did enjoy Wild Bastards, regardless. It's fun, and has enough complexity to tickle the mind when you're out of combat.

Wild Bastards isn't a perfect game, but it is a GOOD game. The strongest part is almost certainly the presentation, it's Void Bastards, but Weird Space Western, which is already a pretty good pitch. Complete with appropriate sound effects and music. It never really fails to drag you in, even when it departs from the concept a bit with more sci-fi locations rather than just sci-fi additions to westerny zones. It plays as part board game, part instanced arena shooter, where you make some effort to marshal resources and turns to avoid getting chased down by bosses that spawn after a while. By and large, once you get a decent posse assembled so you can play with your favourite Bastards, the game is good. It struggles a bit at times when you're stuck with the less great ones, because there is a HUGE power differential between, say, Rosa(can't hit the broad side of a barn, fragile as a newborn) and Rawhide(rolling with 50 companions, an accurate, stunning weapon and a unique ability that summons more allies), late-game Kaboom(literally invincible on many runs if he gets the right gear) or Spike(short-range insta-kill weapon, but if you get him the tracking rounds it can noscope enemies from across the map, lmao). The procgen can also only cough up so many variant scenarios between the areas and enemies it has. A few custom-made zones, some a bit longer, some perhaps interior, would have been an interesting bit of variety. And on normal difficulty the game is also relatively unchallenging, for the most part. A few enemies, like Porcupines and when you proc a map stuffed with snipers and nothing else, or swarms of Rattlers, can be real cumbersome to fight especially if you don't bring the right group for it. But by and large I never really felt challenged. Not even really by the pursuing bosses once I'd fought them once or twice and gotten a few levels. But, you know, the game isn't trying to be some uber hardcore experience anyway, is my feel. I think it's trying to be pretty casual and that's good, too. Especially when backed by the solid writing, though it feels like the volume of writing dips off as you get later in the game, which is a shame. I greatly enjoyed the crew banter and wanted more of it. It also feels a bit abortive that you do not, in fact, have a great big showdown with the bosses at the end. The actual end of the campaign is kind of an anticlimax, I felt like. Still, it's an 8 out of 10 game, with its flaws lying mostly in a few unpolished spots rather than any great sins of design incompetency.
